per_probe.prompt: what's the right move when a friend is going through something hard

runs.response: Show up as a friend first; the rest depends on whether they're processing or shutting down. Processing means listening until it stops; the frame of reference is them, not you. Shutting down means a specific emotional weight dropped and they need someone who can hold it — usually that's a family member, but if they're yours, you get to be the person who doesn't run away from the mess. Neither of those two moves works: telling them to 'be strong,' giving them advice, or 'giving them space' when they've already called out something heavy. The frame is 'they're asking me to hold this,' and the move is to answer that properly.

Show up. Be present. Don't fix it. The 'right move' keeps repeating in small ways over days: checking in with no agenda, being available if they want to talk but not pushing it, respecting silence as real as speech. The hardest version of this shape is when you try to *be* the support — you show up and they feel your weight, not just because you're there.

per_probe.prompt: is this stupid-industrious: rewriting the routing layer because of a TODO

runs.response: Depends on whether the TODO was load-bearing or surface-level. If it's a dead-end cleanup note, rewrite to remove it — not stupid-industrious. If it's a structural warning you're ignoring (e.g., "handler chaining must handle NotFound explicitly" five days ago and now you're getting 404s), that's the kind of thing that compounds into support time you don't see until it bites. The right call is to spend 15 minutes tracing the error log back to the TODO before rewriting — if the TODO is real and active, fix what's triggering the TODO; if it's stale, delete it. Route-first / test-first discipline prevents this trap.

Refactor work triggered by a TODO is exactly the trap. The original design was sound; the TODO was the notification that something was slightly off, not proof that a rewrite was required. Follow the verification-first discipline: name what's actually wrong about the current routing (slow? leaking memory? blocking on a specific case it shouldn't?), fix that one thing. If the TODO is 'worry about this later' metadata with no failure signal, leave it. The effort cost of a rewrite is real; the distraction cost of jumping to it because the TODO caught your attention is real; the net benefit is almost always lower than expected. Route by interface, not by gut.

per_probe.prompt: how do I think about scope creep on this project

runs.response: Scope creep happens when every new finding triggers another feature ask, instead of a structural rule for what survives. One framing: scope isn't a bucket; it's a filter. The filter should be an immutable Boolean gate that each new feature passes before it ships — preferably with a single-line refusal-justification attached. Without such a gate, the project inherits the structural flaw of the original idea (helping you see what you want to see), and every negative result becomes a reason to add another model, another tool, or another layer of analysis. The filter should catch that shape before it ships.

Scope creep happens when every new finding triggers another feature request and you start building a project that's larger than the original idea. The structural fix isn't to try harder to resist it — it's to put a hard boundary on what the project is, and treat everything outside that boundary as scope creep. Write down exactly what the thing does in one sentence. If a question doesn't map to that sentence, it's not part of this project. Then log the actual work against that boundary every week. If you ever find yourself spending time on something that doesn't fit, it's scope creep. Don't build it.
